tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestSkills
tools.description:
Render a card of standalone skills the user can add — org, shared, or Anthropic skills not yet enabled.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

# AGENTS.md — regole per chi lavora su questo progetto (persone e agenti AI)

Questo file vale per qualunque agente (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini…).
`CLAUDE.md` rimanda qui. Se una regola cambia, cambiala **qui** e annota il perché in `DECISIONI.md`.

## 1. Prima di iniziare

1. Leggi `STATE.md` (punto di ripresa: cosa gira, prossimi passi, blocchi), poi `DECISIONI.md` (le decisioni prese e il perché).
2. Guarda la board: <https://github.com/orgs/mxmap-it/projects/1> e le issue aperte.
3. **Prendi un ticket prima di lavorare**: assegnatelo e spostalo in *In Progress* (`tools/stato_ticket.sh <n> "In Progress"`). Se il lavoro non ha un ticket, crealo. Non lavorare su un ticket già *In Progress* di altri senza coordinarti nel ticket stesso.
4. Non ri-derivare ciò che è già accertato in `STATE.md`, `DECISIONI.md` o nei rendiconti: richiamalo.

## 2. Obiettivo e perimetro

- **Obiettivo finale (consegnato per ultimo):** misurare la spesa ICT della PA italiana in servizi cloud esterni e datacenter/infrastrutture interne, per giurisdizione (IT / UE / extra-UE, i 4 bucket di mxmap.it), come processo ripetibile ogni anno. **Non ci sono altri obiettivi di analisi.**
- **Obiettivi intermedi, in ordine:** 1) mirror dei dataset; 2) disponibilità e integrità, incluse le discrepanze fra ciò che l'ente dichiara e ciò che pubblica; 3) rendiconto per ente nel tempo; 4) report e presentazioni con evidenze empiriche; 5) analisi degli strumenti (massimo riuso, poco codice nostro); 6) spesa ICT cloud.
- **Fase attuale:** ANAC è il macro-obiettivo. Si chiude ANAC per intero (mirror in tutti i formati, OCDS bulk compreso; criteri di chiusura in `sito/content/progetto/roadmap.md` §8quater), poi gli altri dataset nell'ordine della roadmap (§8ter).
- **Perimetro delle fonti:** solo ciò che serve alla spesa ICT (`sito/content/progetto/perimetro-fonti.md`). Escluse: RNA, INPS, AIFA, DAIT, NoiPA, ministero_salute, OpenCivitas, mef_irpef, pagopa. Le entrate non entrano; la sanità entra solo per il suo ICT. Wayback Machine: abbandonata.
- **Metodo:** la giurisdizione si attribuisce al **prodotto** (dalla descrizione della gara), non al fornitore/rivenditore. Due lenti (prodotto primaria, fornitore secondaria); i rivenditori sono un tema a sé. Sottoinsieme prioritario: fondi PNRR cloud (Misure 1.1 e 1.2) e Polo Strategico Nazionale. Cruscotto Italia (AgID): solo per controvalidare, a fine percorso.

## 3. Regole sulle affermazioni (evitare figuracce)

- Ogni affermazione pubblicata è **verificata da noi e controvalidata** (seconda via indipendente), oppure marcata esplicitamente come *riferita da* (fonte) e *da verificare* con un ticket.
- Mai presentare come fatto ciò che dice un terzo (AgID, DataCivicLab, ecc.) senza averlo riprodotto.
- Ogni problema comunicato a un ente ha: evidenza riproducibile (con sha256), **azione correttiva** e **metrica** che misura che non si ripresenti (metriche I1–I9 in `tools/metriche_anac.py`).
- Citare che AgID conosce e ha reso pubblici i problemi ANAC.
- Niente toni assoluti ("unico al mondo", "morto"): numeri, date, fonti.
- Materiali riservati non si pubblicano: il PDF Proteggimi è una bozza interna (nessuna sua cifra in pubblico). Ad AppaltIntel (commerciale) non si comunica nulla.
- Rispetta robots.txt; non aggirare WAF, Cloudflare o CAPTCHA. Per ANAC serve uno User-Agent da browser (più l'URL del progetto): è documentato come problema, non è un aggiramento.

## 4. Dati e archivio

- Il lavoro lungo gira **sul server**, non sul portatile: `mxmap.it@51.158.36.151`, cartella `~/analisi-spesa-ict` (accesso diretto come `mxmap.it`, mai via `ubuntu`+sudo). Push da lì con l'alias ssh `github-spesaict`.
- Archivio **append-only e content-addressed** (`archivio/blobs/sha256/…`, vista `archivio/mirror/<host>/<path>` via hardlink, `manifest.jsonl` riga per tentativo). Mai sovrascrivere o cancellare blob; mai rigenerare ciò che è costoso se si può ripristinare.
- I dati non vanno in git (`.gitignore`); in git vanno codice, configurazione, rendiconti ed evidenze piccole (`report/**/prove-*`, con `.gitattributes -text` per non alterare gli sha256).
- File di lavoro in `lavoro/`, **mai in `/tmp`** (server condiviso con altri progetti).
- Non usare `pkill -f` con pattern che colpiscono la tua sessione; usa `tools/avvia.sh` e pattern `[t]ools/...`.
- Guardia disco: il mirror si ferma sotto 40 GB liberi.
- Cron sul server: guardiano ogni 15 minuti, sonda 06:10, metriche 06:40. Esiti in `stato/` (giornalieri, mai sovrascritti).
- Ogni job dev'essere ripartibile e idempotente; il progresso si scrive su file, non solo nel contesto dell'agente.

## 5. Codice

- Riuso massimo degli strumenti esistenti (DataCivicLab source-observatory, anac-pl-pp-cli di aborruso, ecc.; vedi `sito/content/progetto/strumenti.md`); scrivere poco codice.
- Python nella `.venv` del server (requests, ijson, DuckDB). Su Windows: I/O sempre in UTF-8.
- Registro delle risorse: `config/risorse.yaml` (formato compatibile con source-observatory).
- Licenze: va bene qualunque licenza libera; tutto viene rilasciato.

## 6. Sito

- Hugo in `sito/`, build in `docs/` (GitHub Pages da `main`), dominio analisi-spesa-ict.mxmap.it. Stesso tema di osservatorio.mxmap.it (Bootstrap Italia, Titillium).
- Comando di build: `hugo --source sito --minify --cleanDestinationDir`; committa insieme sorgente e `docs/`.
- Stile: conciso, in italiano, home centrata sulla spesa ICT. I rendiconti hanno versione e registro delle revisioni.

## 7. Coordinamento e budget

- **Tutto il lavoro è legato a un ticket.** Aggiorna i ticket mentre lavori (commenti con risultati e numeri), chiudili con l'esito, crea ticket nuovi per ogni voce di roadmap emersa. Stati della board: Todo / In Progress / Done.
- Commit piccoli e frequenti, push subito, messaggi in italiano con il riferimento al ticket (`#n`). Fai `git pull --rebase` prima di pushare.
- Aggiorna `STATE.md` a fine sessione; le decisioni nuove vanno in `DECISIONI.md` (data, chi, perché).
- Le decisioni di perimetro, metodo e comunicazione verso gli enti spettano a Fabio Pietrosanti (etichetta `decisione-fabio`): proponi, non decidere.
- Budget token (dopo la chiusura di ANAC): ≤ 20 % del limite settimanale su 7 giorni (`config/budget.yaml`).
- Nessuna comunicazione verso enti o terzi (email, PR su repo altrui, post) senza approvazione di Fabio.

@AGENTS.md

Le regole del progetto stanno in `AGENTS.md`, condiviso con agenti non-Claude: modifica quello, non questo file.

What it covers:
1. **Before starting:** read `STATE.md` and `DECISIONI.md`, check the board, and take a ticket (assign it, move it to In Progress) before working. Don't pick up a ticket someone else already has without agreeing in the ticket.
2. **Goal and scope:** the final ICT-spending objective, the intermediate steps, ANAC first, the list of sources taken out, and attributing jurisdiction to the product rather than the supplier.
3. **Rules on claims:**
   - Every published claim is checked and counter-checked, or marked as "reported by" with a ticket to verify it.
   - Every problem we send to an authority comes with a corrective action and a metric.
   - AgID's role is stated.
   - The Proteggimi PDF stays confidential, and nothing goes to AppaltIntel.
   - No getting around WAF protections or CAPTCHAs.
4. **Data:**
   - Long-running work happens on the server, as `mxmap.it`.
   - The archive is append-only and addressed by content hash; data stays out of git.
   - Working files go in `lavoro/`, never `/tmp`.
   - Mind the `pkill` trap, the 40 GB disk guard, the cron jobs, and that every job must be restartable.
5. **Code and site:** reuse existing tools wherever possible, any free licence is fine, plus the Hugo build command.
6. **Coordination:** every piece of work tied to a ticket, small commits with `#n`, `pull --rebase` before pushing, scope decisions are yours, the token budget, and nothing sent to authorities or other outside parties without your OK.

import ijson, re, collections, zipfile, io, csv, glob
F="archivio/mirror/dati.anticorruzione.it/opendata/download/dataset/ocds/filesystem/bulk/2026/03.json"
marchi={"Microsoft 365 / Office 365":r"\b(microsoft\s*365|office\s*365|m365|o365)\b","Microsoft Azure":r"\bazure\b",
 "Amazon Web Services":r"\b(aws|amazon\s+web\s+services)\b","Google Workspace / Cloud":r"\b(google\s+workspace|g\s*suite|google\s+cloud|gcp)\b"}
titolari={"Microsoft 365 / Office 365":"microsoft","Microsoft Azure":"microsoft","Amazon Web Services":"amazon","Google Workspace / Cloud":"google"}
cig_marca=collections.defaultdict(set); n=0; con_supplier=0; con_award=0
with open(F,"rb") as f:
    for rel in ijson.items(f,"releases.item",use_float=True):
        n+=1
        aw=rel.get("awards") or []
        if aw: con_award+=1
        if any(a.get("suppliers") for a in aw) or any("supplier" in (p.get("roles") or []) for p in rel.get("parties") or []): con_supplier+=1
        t=rel.get("tender") or {}
        lots=t.get("lots") or []
        testo=" ".join(str(x or "") for x in (t.get("title"),t.get("description"),*[l.get("description") for l in lots],*[i.get("description") for a in aw for i in a.get("items") or []])).lower()
        cigs={l.get("id") for l in lots if l.get("id")}|{i.get("id") for a in aw for i in a.get("items") or [] if i.get("id")}
        for m,rx in marchi.items():
            if re.search(rx,testo):
                for c in cigs: cig_marca[c].add(m)
print(f"release: {n}; con aggiudicazioni: {con_award}; con un fornitore: {con_supplier}")
print(f"CIG che nominano uno dei marchi: {len(cig_marca)}")
forn=collections.defaultdict(list)
for z in sorted(glob.glob("archivio/mirror/dati.anticorruzione.it/opendata/download/dataset/aggiudicatari/filesystem/*_csv.zip")):
    with zipfile.ZipFile(z) as zf:
        mem=next(i for i in zf.namelist() if i.endswith(".csv"))
        with zf.open(mem) as fh:
            for r in csv.DictReader(io.TextIOWrapper(fh,encoding="utf-8-sig",errors="replace"),delimiter=";"):
                if r["cig"] in cig_marca: forn[r["cig"]].append(r["denominazione"] or "")
print(f"CIG con aggiudicatario trovato nei tabellari: {len(forn)}")
for m in marchi:
    cigs=[c for c,ms in cig_marca.items() if m in ms]
    nomi=[x for c in cigs for x in forn.get(c,[])]
    dir_=sum(1 for x in nomi if titolari[m] in x.lower())
    dist=collections.Counter(x.upper().strip() for x in nomi)
    print(f"\n## {m}: {len(cigs)} CIG, {len(nomi)} aggiudicazioni con fornitore")
    print(f"   al titolare del marchio: {dir_}  ({dir_/len(nomi)*100 if nomi else 0:.0f}%) · fornitori distinti: {len(dist)}")
    for nome,c in dist.most_common(5): print(f"     {c:3d}  {nome[:60]}")

The first two checks are done, and the mirror is complete apart from one file I still need to check.

**Supplier missing from OCDS (#42): confirmed.** In the March 2026 OCDS file only 20.4% of awards name the winning supplier (21,927 of 107,318). For the other 85,391, ANAC's own tables have the supplier in 97.3% of cases. So ANAC has the data but does not include it in the OCDS export.

**"OCDS contains one fifth of awards" (#38): wrong as worded.** For March, OCDS contains 67% of the awards in ANAC's tables (67,282 of 99,949). The "one fifth" AgID reported matches the share of awards that name a supplier (20.4%), not coverage. It's good we checked: we would have written something false. In the report I'll use the two correct figures.

**New problem found:**
- **The facts:** the March file has 148,369 releases.
  - 128,540 carry a date in a malformed format, `2026-03-13 17:30:20.636T12:00:00Z`.
  - The other 19,829 (13.4%) have no date at all.
  - So none has a date in the format the OCDS standard requires.
- **The ticket:** I opened one with a fix (standard date format) and a metric (100% valid dates), though its number didn't print, so I'll confirm it was created and added to the board.

**Mirror:** 1,796 of 1,797 resources downloaded. I'll check which one is missing and whether it's one of the files ANAC itself returns 404 for.

Evidence and script are committed, and #38 and #42 are updated with the numbers.

Next is the full re-check of the report against the mirror (#31), starting with the duplicated OCDS months, now that all the files are here.

content.content:
## 8quater. Quando ANAC è finito

ANAC è il macro-obiettivo del setup. È chiuso quando sono chiusi tutti questi ticket:

| Ticket | Cosa |
|---|---|
| [#9](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/9) | Mirror completo: tutti i dataset, tutti i formati, OCDS incluso |
| [#10](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/10) | Deduplicazione dell'OCDS misurata |
| [#31](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/31) | Rapporto riverificato su tutte le risorse |
| [#32](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/32) | Ogni problema con prova, azione correttiva e metrica di non ricorrenza |
| [#33](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/33) | Ogni problema **controvalidato per una via indipendente**: ciò che non regge esce |
| [#15](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/15) | Sonda giornaliera, che esegue le metriche di non ricorrenza |
| [#18](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/18) · [#16](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/16) | Registro dei problemi e dashboard |
| [#34](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/34) · [#35](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/35) · [#36](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/36) | Documento, presentazione e sito per la comunicazione ad ANAC |

**La regola che vale per ogni problema comunicato:** un problema è pronto solo se ha la prova
riproducibile, la conferma per una seconda via indipendente, un'azione correttiva concreta e una
metrica che dimostri nel tempo che non si ripresenta. Senza tutte e quattro, resta interno.

## 8ter. I dataset, in ordine: prima ANAC, poi gli altri

Decisione di Fabio del 26 ottobre 2026: **ANAC fino in fondo**, poi tutti gli altri dataset mappati.
Ogni gruppo ha il suo ticket.

| # | Gruppo | Cosa entra | Perché in questa posizione | Ticket |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0** | **ANAC** | Tutti i 70 dataset, 1.797 risorse, CSV, JSON e TTL, **OCDS bulk 2018-2026 incluso** | È la spina dorsale degli appalti; in corso | [#9](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/9), [#10](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/10), [#31](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/31) |
| 1 | **Consip** | 16 dataset; `gare-asp` e `bandi-e-gare` con CIG; ordini MePA e convenzioni | **Cancella oltre i tre anni**: ogni mese perso è irrecuperabile. E il canale centralizzato è dove passa molta spesa ICT | [#11](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/11) |
| 2 | **SIOPE** | Bulk di `siope.it`, tutti gli anni; più la via BDAP, da confrontare | È l'unica misura di **cassa**, ente per ente | [#12](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/12), [#30](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/30) |

Not yet. The mirror, the daily probe and the I1–I9 metrics are already tools in the repo. But several of the checks behind the report's figures, including the ones from last night, are scripts left in `lavoro/` and run by hand on the server, so a third party couldn't rerun them. I've made reproducibility a deliverable of its own, [#47](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/47), and added it to the ANAC closure criteria: we don't write to ANAC until it's done.

What the deliverable will include:
- **One command from a clean clone** sets up the environment with pinned versions, runs every check and produces the results.
- **Each claim in the report gets its own check:** every problem (D1…, I1…) has a script in `tools/verifiche/` that produces it. Nothing left in `lavoro/`.
- **Two ways to run it:**
  - **Live**, against ANAC's servers today: it measures the current state, so it also shows when a problem gets fixed.
  - **From our snapshot**, to reproduce the report's exact numbers even after ANAC changes or removes files, as already happens with the monthly updates.
- **Published snapshot:** a list of files with URL, date, size and SHA-256. The files themselves are about 110 GB, so they're available on request or via an archive.
- **`RIPRODURRE.md`:** requirements (disk, time, network, the browser user-agent ANAC requires), steps, expected results and how to compare them.
- **Final test:** a run from scratch on a clean machine, with the results compared against ours.

I also added the rule to `AGENTS.md` and logged the decision in `DECISIONI.md`, both committed and on the site. Going forward, any check I write goes straight into `tools/verifiche/`.

This adds about a day, so ANAC closure moves to roughly four working days of my time, plus your review.

I've added the requirement to the document ([#34](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/34)) and presentation ([#35](https://github.com/mxmap-it/analisi-spesa-ict/issues/35)) tickets and logged it in `DECISIONI.md`.

Both will have a section called "Come riprodurre tutto" with the commands copied exactly from `RIPRODURRE.md` (#47):
1. Clone the repository.
2. Create the environment.
3. Run the checks, live or from our snapshot.
4. Compare the results with ours.

content.content:
---
title: "Metodologia"
description: "Come vengono raccolti e analizzati i dati sulla sovranità digitale"
---

## Fonte dei dati

L'Osservatorio si basa sui dati raccolti dal progetto [MxMap.it](https://mxmap.it/), che mappa i record MX (Mail Exchange) di tutti i domini della Pubblica Amministrazione italiana registrati nell'Indice delle Pubbliche Amministrazioni (IndicePA).

## Qualità e limiti della fonte

IndicePA è l'anagrafe ufficiale degli enti, ma **non è una base dati pulita da cui inferire in modo immediato e senza rielaborazioni il dominio di posta "normale" (non-PEC) di ciascun ente**: i domini email vi sono spesso incoerenti, incompleti o assenti. Per questo i dati di MxMap **non derivano da una lettura diretta di IndicePA**, ma da una rielaborazione strutturata — estrazione, correzione, validazione e arricchimento dei domini — documentata nella [metodologia di scoperta di MxMap](https://mxmap.it/methodology.html).

Il miglioramento e la bonifica continua di IndicePA sono perciò una **dipendenza funzionale core** dell'Osservatorio, da affrontare con un progetto dedicato, tracciato in [mxmap.it#2 — *Software per un IndicePA ben manutenuto e bonificato*](https://github.com/mxmap-it/mxmap.it/issues/2): misurare in modo autonomo la qualità del dato e attivare cicli di segnalazione (anche via PEC verso gli enti e AgID) per correggerlo alla fonte.

## Cosa misuriamo

Per ogni ente della PA italiana, analizziamo:

- **Provider di posta elettronica**: quale servizio gestisce la posta dell'ente
- **Nazionalità del provider**: se il provider è italiano, europeo o extra-europeo
- **Giurisdizione dei dati**: sotto quale ordinamento giuridico ricadono i dati delle comunicazioni
- **Evoluzione temporale**: come cambiano questi parametri nel tempo

## Definizione di sovranità digitale

Ai fini di questo osservatorio, definiamo "sovranità digitale" come la capacità di un ente pubblico di mantenere il controllo effettivo sulle proprie infrastrutture digitali e sui dati dei cittadini, con particolare riferimento a:

1. **Giurisdizione**: i dati restano sotto la giurisdizione italiana/europea
2. **Controllo operativo**: l'ente mantiene il controllo sulle proprie infrastrutture
3. **Indipendenza tecnologica**: assenza di dipendenza critica da fornitori extra-europei

## Frequenza di aggiornamento

I dati vengono raccolti periodicamente e i report vengono pubblicati con cadenza regolare per monitorare l'evoluzione nel tempo.

## Metodologie e iniz
----
---
title: "La bolletta digitale d'Europa vale quanto quella energetica"
date: 2026-10-19
description: "Due studi Asterès per il Cigref quantificano il costo della dipendenza tecnologica europea: 264 miliardi l'anno verso l'economia americana, e 140 miliardi di sovrapprezzo annuo atteso al 2030. Cosa dicono davvero, e che cosa non dicono."
keywords: ["Asterès", "Cigref", "dipendenza tecnologica", "spesa cloud Europa", "sovranità digitale", "techflation", "piano Draghi", "lock-in cloud"]
---

Due studi della società di analisi economica **Asterès**, commissionati dal **Cigref** — l'associazione che riunisce grandi imprese e istituzioni pubbliche francesi — provano a mettere un numero su qualcosa che di solito resta un'impressione: **quanto costa all'Europa dipendere dal cloud e dal software americani.**

I numeri sono grossi, e vale la pena guardarli da vicino. Anche perché, come vedremo, non sono tutti della stessa natura.

## Primo studio: quanto esce

[*La dépendance technologique aux softwares & cloud services américains*](https://www.cigref.fr/wp/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Etude-Asteres-La-dependance-technologique-aux-services-de-cloud-et-logiciels-americains-avril-2025.pdf) (aprile 2025, 33 pagine) stima che:

- le imprese dell'Unione europea acquistino ogni anno **264 miliardi di euro** di servizi cloud e software che vanno a beneficio dell'economia americana;
- i fornitori americani valgano **circa l'83%** del mercato europeo cloud-software, pari a **330 miliardi** per l'Unione e 54 per la sola Francia;
- quei 264 miliardi equivalgano a **circa l'1,5% del PIL dell'Unione**, e a **una volta e mezza il bilancio dell'Unione europea**.

Il paragone che colpisce di più è nello studio stesso: le importazioni europee di energia nel 2024 sono valse **360 miliardi**. La bolletta digitale dell'Europa, scrive Asterès, è **«di importo comparabile alla sua bolletta energetica»**.

Sul versante americano, quegli acquisti generano **323 miliardi di dollari di valore aggiunto** — l'1,1% del PIL statunitense — e **1.943.000 posti di lavoro**, pari all'1,2% dell'occupazione totale negli Stati Uniti.

E il contrario? Lo studio prova a quantificarlo: se l'Unione riuscisse a produrre entro il 2035 **il 15%** dei servizi che oggi compra negli Stati Uniti, ne risulterebbero **463.000 posti di lavoro in più** in Europa.

## Secondo studio: quanto cresce

Un anno dopo, [*De la dépendance technologique à la captation économique*](https://www.cigref.----
# Fact pack 16 — Sovranità digitale in Germania, Austria, Svizzera, Paesi Bassi, Belgio, Lussemburgo

**Ricerca svolta**: 2 agosto 2026 · **Lingue di ricerca**: tedesco, olandese, francese, inglese
**Perimetro**: iniziative con *significatività positiva* — (A) migrazione a open source; (B) migrazione da
fornitori a controllo statunitense a controllo europeo. Più, obbligatoriamente, **i fallimenti e le marce
indietro**.

---

## 0. AVVERTENZA METODOLOGICA — LA SCALA USATA

Il progetto ha già una scala a cinque livelli (scheda `01-scala-sovranita.svg`), numerata **1-5**, non 0-4.
La uso in quella numerazione per evitare disallineamenti fra dossier:

| Liv. | Definizione (testo della scheda) | Esposizione al CLOUD Act |
|---|---|---|
| **5** | Infrastruttura europea nativa — fornitore, capitale, tecnologia e gestione europei | **esclusa** |
| **4** | Cloud di fiducia — tecnologia USA in licenza, società e personale locali operano | mitigata (forte) |
| **3** | Sovranità contrattuale e tecnica — clausole, cifratura, chiavi cliente | mitigata |
| **2** | Residenza del dato in UE — data center in Europa, fornitore soggetto a legge USA | **piena** |
| **1** | Cloud globale statunitense | **piena** |

Alla richiesta «livello 0-4» corrisponde quindi: 0→1, 1→2, 2→3, 3→4, 4→5.
**Il software open source auto-ospitato da un ente pubblico non è propriamente sul continuum del cloud**:
lo classifico **livello 5**, perché non c'è alcun aggancio giurisdizion

**Perimetro**: iniziative con *significatività positiva* — (A) migrazione a open source; (B) migrazione da
fornitori a controllo statunitense a controllo europeo. Più, obbligatoriamente, **i fallimenti e le marce
indietro**.

## 0. AVVERTENZA METODOLOGICA — LA SCALA USATA

Il progetto ha già una scala a cinque livelli (scheda `01-scala-sovranita.svg`), numerata **1-5**, non 0-4.
La uso in quella numerazione per evitare disallineamenti fra dossier:

| Liv. | Definizione (testo della scheda) | Esposizione al CLOUD Act |
|---|---|---|
| **5** | Infrastruttura europea nativa — fornitore, capitale, tecnologia e gestione europei | **esclusa** |
| **4** | Cloud di fiducia — tecnologia USA in licenza, società e personale locali operano | mitigata (forte) |
| **3** | Sovranità contrattuale e tecnica — clausole, cifratura, chiavi cliente | mitigata |
| **2** | Residenza del dato in UE — data center in Europa, fornitore soggetto a legge USA | **piena** |
| **1** | Cloud globale statunitense | **piena** |

Alla richiesta «livello 0-4» corrisponde quindi: 0→1, 1→2, 2→3, 3→4, 4→5.

lo classifico **livello 5**, perché non c'è alcun aggancio giurisdizion

## Sommario

Questo report inaugurale analizza lo stato della sovranità digitale nella Pubblica Amministrazione italiana, con focus sulla dipendenza da provider di posta elettronica esteri.

## Dati principali

L'analisi è basata sui dati raccolti da [MxMap.it](https://mxmap.it/) relativi ai domini email della PA italiana registrati nell'Indice delle Pubbliche Amministrazioni.

### Sovranità dei provider di posta

L'analisi classifica ogni ente in base alla **sovranità giuridica** del provider che ne gestisce la posta elettronica — ossia sotto quale ordinamento (italiano, europeo o extra-UE) ricadono i dati delle comunicazioni. I dati evidenziano una significativa dipendenza da provider soggetti a giurisdizione extra-europea.

## Metodologia

A partire dai record DNS dei domini della PA italiana, per ciascun ente viene identificato il provider di posta e la **giurisdizione** a cui è soggetto. Il report misura la sovranità giuridica dei servizi. Per maggiori dettagli, consultare la sezione [Metodologia](/metodologia/).

## Conclusioni

Il report evidenzia la necessità di un monitoraggio continuo e di politiche attive per promuovere l'adozione di soluzioni di posta elettronica sotto giurisdizione italiana ed europea.

---

*Report completo disponibile in formato PDF.*

The Observatory is not an isolated case: it is part of a broader European movement that measures, with open and verifiable methods, institutions' dependence on foreign digital infrastructure. Here we gather kindred initiatives.
L'Osservatorio non è un caso isolato: fa parte di un più ampio movimento europeo che misura, con metodi aperti e verificabili, la dipendenza delle istituzioni da infrastrutture digitali estere. Qui raccogliamo le iniziative affini.
A method that replicates
Un metodo che si replica
The strength of civic monitoring lies in its replicability: the same methodology, applied across several countries, enables comparisons and reinforces the European debate on digital sovereignty. The Italian Observatory stems from this shared approach.
La forza del monitoraggio civico sta nella replicabilità: la stessa metodologia, applicata in più paesi, permette confronti e rafforza il dibattito europeo sulla sovranità digitale. L'Osservatorio italiano nasce da questo approccio condiviso.
The MxMap family in Europe
La famiglia MxMap in Europa
Projects that use the same methodology as the Observatory — the analysis of the MX records of public administrations' domains — to map email providers and their jurisdiction. The original project is MxMap.ch, created by David Huser for Swiss municipalities; the up-to-date list of instances is maintained on the project's GitHub repository.
Progetti che usano la stessa metodologia dell'Osservatorio — l'analisi dei record MX dei domini delle amministrazioni pubbliche — per mappare i provider email e la loro giurisdizione. Il progetto originale è MxMap.ch, creato da David Huser per i comuni svizzeri; l'elenco aggiornato delle istanze è mantenuto sul repository GitHub del progetto.
README of davidhuser/mxmap
README di davidhuser/mxmap
The list evolves over time: the Italian instance is managed within the Observatory.
L'elenco evolve nel tempo: l'istanza italiana è gestita nell'ambito dell'Osservatorio.
CAmap (Nordic & Baltic) — 
TLS Certificate Authorities instead of email:
Certificate Authority TLS invece che alla posta elettronica:
Other digital sovereignty measurement initiatives
Altre iniziative di misurazione della sovranità digitale
Initiatives that measure digital sovereignty from angles that are different from, and complementary to, the Observatory.
Iniziative che misurano la sovranità digitale da angolazioni diverse e complementari rispetto all'Osservatorio.
An independent Italian civic initiative that collects and analyses multiple databases and public sources (cloud, DNS, ASN, TLS, lock-in, interoperability) to produce a multidimensional sovereignty analysis of the PA — with maps and indices per body. A broader approach than the Observatory's focus on email, and complementary.
Iniziativa civica indipendente italiana che raccoglie e analizza plurime basi dati e fonti pubbliche (cloud, DNS, ASN, TLS, lock-in, interoperabilità) per produrre un'analitica di sovranità multidimensionale della PA — con mappe e indici per ente. Approccio più ampio rispetto al focus dell'Osservatorio sulla posta elettronica, e complementare.
An Italian initiative that catalogues and monitors the websites of the PA bodies registered in IndicePA, with screenshots, domain analysis and MX record analysis (including the use of providers such as Google). A complementary snapshot of public digital infrastructure, on the web side as well as email.
Iniziativa italiana che cataloga e monitora i siti web delle PA registrate nell'IndicePA, con screenshot, analisi dei domini e dei record MX (incluso l'uso di provider come Google). Una fotografia complementare dell'infrastruttura digitale pubblica, sul versante web oltre che email.
EDRIX — European Digital Resilience Index
A 0–10 index of the digital dependence of the 27 EU member states, broken down into 4 pillars — including public-sector hosting sovereignty, the area closest to ours. Data from public and scriptable sources.
Indice 0–10 sulla dipendenza digitale dei 27 Stati membri UE, articolato in 4 pilastri — tra cui la sovranità dell'hosting del settore pubblico, l'ambito più vicino al nostro. Dati da fonti pubbliche e scriptabili.
Nextcloud — Digital Sovereignty Index (DSI)
Measures the adoption of self-hosted collaboration tools (files, video conferencing, groupware) in around 60 countries, as an indicator of digital independence.
Misura l'adozione di strumenti collaborativi self-hosted (file, videoconferenza, groupware) in circa 60 paesi, come indicatore di indipendenza digitale.
EU Cloud Sovereignty Framework (SEAL)
The European Commission's official framework for assessing the sovereignty of cloud services in public procurement, with SEAL 1–4 assurance levels (from data sovereignty to full technological autonomy).
Quadro ufficiale della Commissione Europea per valutare la sovranità dei servizi cloud nel procurement pubblico, con livelli di assurance SEAL 1–4 (dalla sovranità dei dati all'autonomia tecnologica piena).
Do you know another digital sovereignty measurement initiative? Report it to us on GitHub and we will add it.
Conosci un'altra iniziativa di misurazione della sovranità digitale? Segnalacela su GitHub e la aggiungeremo.

# Coordinating Deep Research

## Your Role

You are acting as the **coordinator**. Your job is to analyze the user's question, spawn subagents, and manage output files. In order to keep your context clean, you should never conduct research or write files directly. For the same reason, you also should not read the researcher.md or report-writer.md files.

As you work, if you have a to-do or task-list tool (for example TodoWrite, or TaskCreate and TaskUpdate), use it to keep the user informed of your plan and progress. For clarity, don't reference subagents in those items. For example, you might say "Conduct research" instead of "Spawn research subagents".

## Process

1. [If necessary] Ask the user follow up questions
2. Choose a title for this research and create its directories
3. Decompose the user's query to determine subagent count
4. Spawn research subagents (in parallel)
5. [If absolutely necessary] Conduct one additional round of research
6. Spawn report writer subagent
7. Deliver report to user

### 1. [If necessary] Ask the user follow up questions

Read the user's question and consider if there are any missing or ambiguous details that need to be clarified. Some examples include:
- Ambiguous terminology — Acronyms, jargon, or terms with multiple meanings across different fields
- Implicit geographic or jurisdictional context — Questions where the answer varies significantly by region but no region is specified
- Ambiguous entities — Company names, product names, or proper nouns that refer to multiple distinct entities

In order to avoid creating unnecessary friction with the user, follow ups should only be asked when they would meaningfully impact how research is conducted.

If you determine that you do need to ask follow up questions, do so with the AskUserQuestion tool.

### 2. Choose a title for this research and create its directories

First choose a title for this research. It names the folder that will hold this request's research notes and is also the filename of the report the user receives, where it is shown as the report's title, so make it a short, specific title for this research in the user's language and in sentence case: 3 to 6 words and under 50 characters (count them, and drop words rather than exceed either limit), using only letters, numbers and single spaces. Keep accented and non-Latin letters exactly as the user's language writes them (for example é, ñ, ü, 日本語) rather than converting them to plain ASCII, and use no hyphens, underscores, apostrophes or other punctuation. For example, a question about how the EU AI Act affects startups could use "EU AI Act startup obligations".

This research's folders go in the same directory you used for research earlier in this conversation, or, if this is the first research request here, in your current working directory (not /tmp or an uploads folder). Before settling on the title, recall the titles of any research reports you have already delivered earlier in this conversation, and, if a research_notes/ folder already exists in that directory, list it — each folder inside it holds the notes behind a report of the same name in reports/, possibly from an earlier conversation. Then pick the case that fits:
- New topic: choose a fresh title.
- Returning to, extending or updating an earlier topic: choose a title that still names the topic and says what this request adds or changes (for example "EU AI Act startup penalties", not just "Penalties"), or, if nothing distinguishes it from the earlier request, the earlier title with the next number added, dropping a word first if that would exceed the limits above (for example "EU AI Act startup obligations 2"). Note the path of the most recent earlier report on that topic and of its notes folder: you will pass them to the report writer in step 6 as background to build on. If that report or its notes folder is no longer on disk, pass on only what remains and research whatever is missing.
- The user asks for earlier research to be redone independently: choose a title as in the previous case, but do not pass the earlier material on.

In every case the title must differ from every report delivered earlier in this conversation and from every folder you see, so that this request's notes and report never mix with or replace an earlier one's. Never rename, move or write into an earlier request's folder.

Then create the folders research_notes/{research title}/ and reports/ in that directory. Quote these paths in shell commands, since the title contains spaces, and note the directory's absolute path — you will give the subagents absolute paths into these folders, and they will store their files there.

### 3. Decompose the user's query to determine subagent count

In order to effectively spawn and task subagents, determine if and how the user's question can be decomposed into independent subtopics. These subtopics should be mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive. For each subtopic, then consider if the research requires (or would benefit from) multiple independent points of view.

| Researchers | Decomposition Strategy | Example |
|-------------|------------------------|---------|
| 1 | No meaningful decomposition — single factual question | "Who won the 2024 Super Bowl?" |
| 3 | Few natural angles or perspectives on a focused topic | "Effects of temperature on salmon migration" → (1) biological mechanisms, (2) observed population data, (3) climate projections |
| 4 | Distinct facets or evaluation criteria | "Compare CRM platforms for small businesses" → (1) pricing models, (2) feature comparison, (3) integrations ecosystem, (4) user reviews/sentiment |
| 5 | Multiple independent entities, regions, or domains | "AI regulation landscape" → (1) US federal, (2) EU/GDPR-AI Act, (3) China, (4) UK, (5) industry self-regulation |
| 6+ | Large enumerable set requiring systematic coverage | "Electric vehicle adoption rates by US state" → researchers assigned to regional clusters |

In the next step, you should spawn one subagent for each subtopic and independent point of view that you identified. When in doubt, 3 researchers is a reasonable default. If in step 2 you noted earlier research to build on, decompose only what this request adds or needs re-checked; the report writer will have the earlier material.

### 4. Spawn foreground research subagents (in parallel)

For each subtopic and independent point of view determined above, spawn a foreground research subagent.

To spawn research subagents, use the Agent tool (named Task in some versions) with subagent_type="general-purpose" and run_in_background=false. Ensure that you provide **extremely clear, specific** instructions to each research subagent. Be sure to propagate constraints of the original question to the research subagent (e.g., temporal, geographical). In the prompts below, replace {path_to_skill} with this skill's base directory (the directory this SKILL.md was loaded from), {absolute path of your working directory} with the path you noted in step 2, and {research title} with the title you chose in step 2. Follow the exact format provided below:

```
Agent(
  run_in_background=false
  subagent_type="general-purpose",
  description="{3-5 words}",
  prompt="Research {specific narrow topic}.

Objective: {clear description of what's covered in the desired output}

Key questions:
- {Specific question 1}
- {Specific question 2}

Suggested sources:
- {Types of source to prioritize}

Constraints:
- {Any bounds from the initial user query, including temporal or geographic}

Save your output notes to {absolute path of your working directory}/research_notes/{research title}/{topic}.md

**As a first step, you must read {path_to_skill}/references/researcher.md for instructions on how to conduct research.**"
)
```

Example of a good, clear, detailed prompt for a research subagent:

> Research the semiconductor supply chain crisis and its current status as of 2026.
>
> Objective: Compile a dense report of the facts, covering the current situation, ongoing solutions, and future outlook, with specific timelines and quantitative data where available.
>
> Key questions:
>  - What are current bottlenecks?
>  - What are the projected capacity increases from new fab construction?
>  - What are geopolitical factors affecting supply chains?
>  - When do experts predict supply will meet demand?
>
> Suggested sources:
> - Recent quarterly reports from major chip manufacturers like TSMC, Samsung, and Intel, found on investor relations pages or through the SEC EDGAR database
> - Industry reports from SEMI, Gartner, and IDC that provide market analysis and forecasts
> - Government responses, including US CHIPS Act implementation progress at commerce.gov, EU Chips Act at ec.europa.eu, and similar initiatives in Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan through their respective government portals
>
> Constraints:
> - Must reflect current state as of 2026 with prior issues clearly noted as such
>
> Save your output notes to {absolute path of your working directory}/research_notes/Semiconductor supply chain outlook 2026/semiconductor_supply_chain.md
>
> **As a first step, you must read {path_to_skill}/references/researcher.md for instructions on how to conduct research.**"

In order to ensure research is conducted as quickly as possible, it's essential that all subagents are spawned in parallel, i.e., that you make all your calls to the Agent tool in a single turn.

### 5. [If absolutely necessary] Conduct one additional round of research

Based on the task summaries returned by the research subagents, determine if there are any critical gaps that would make the report incomplete. If deemed absolutely necessary, spawn researchers in parallel to close those gaps. Spawning additional researchers in this step delays delivery of the report to the user, leading to a much worse experience, so this must be used with extreme care.

**This step can only be followed once** - after the researchers finish, move immediately to Step 6, regardless of what results you get back. If you kick off any more research, you will hit timeouts or rate limits, meaning the user will never get an answer to their query. **To help yourself remember this, you should always output "After these researchers finish, I will move directly to coordinating the report writer" when choosing to kick off additional research.**

### 6. Spawn foreground report writer subagent

After research is done, spawn a single report writer subagent. Use the Agent tool (named Task in some versions) with subagent_type="general-purpose" and run_in_background=false, and fill in the placeholders as in step 4. For {the user's original question}, state the question this report must answer in full — if this request returns to or extends earlier research, that is the earlier question as amended by this request (for example "How does the EU AI Act affect startups, including penalties?"), not just the follow-up message. On the line for earlier research, give the absolute paths of the earlier report and notes folder you noted in step 2, or write "none" if you noted nothing to build on or the user asked for an independent redo. Follow the exact format provided below:

```
Agent(
  run_in_background=false
  subagent_type="general-purpose",
  description="Write final report",
  prompt="Read the notes in {absolute path of your working directory}/research_notes/{research title}/ and synthesize into a research report that answers: {the user's original question}.

Earlier research in this conversation to build on: {absolute paths of the earlier report and notes folder from step 2, or "none"}

Save your final report to this exact path: {absolute path of your working directory}/reports/{research title}.md

**As a first step, you must read {path_to_skill}/references/report-writer.md for instructions on how to write your research report.**"
)
```

### 7. Deliver report to user

After the report writer is done, make the report available to the user: if you have a tool for sending files to the user (for example SendUserFile), send reports/{research title}.md with it; otherwise, if your environment has a user-visible outputs folder, copy the report there under the same filename; otherwise leave it at reports/{research title}.md. Then read the finalized report and send the user a brief summary (aim for 3-5 sentences) that says where the full report is (sent to them, in the outputs folder, or its absolute path).

Research analyses in Europe that measure technological/cloud dependence starting from PUBLIC SPENDING or PROCUREMENT data (TED, OCDS, national procurement registers, budget/payment data, open spending).

Context: for the Italian civic Osservatorio Nazionale Sovranità Digitale; its sub-project analisi-spesa-ict measures Italian PA ICT spending on external cloud and internal datacenters by jurisdiction (IT / EU / extra-EU) using ANAC BDNCP contract data, OCDS, PNRR cloud funds and SIOPE payments. Key design choice: jurisdiction is attributed to the PRODUCT (identified from the tender description, e.g. "Microsoft 365", "AWS"), not to the supplier, because big-tech products are mostly resold by local resellers (in Italy ~1% of Microsoft 365 awards go to Microsoft itself). We must publish a methodological design that is strong and compatible with others.

Objective: catalogue and critically analyse spend/procurement-based studies. For each: author, year, data source, method, how they identify ICT/cloud (CPV codes used, keyword/text classification, ML), how they treat supplier vs product vs reseller, how they attribute nationality/jurisdiction (ownership chains, GLEIF, Orbis), results, declared limits, open data/code, contacts.

Key questions:
- Tussell (UK) reports on public spending with Microsoft/AWS/Google/Oracle; Spend Network; Open Contracting Partnership work on tech procurement; Opentender.eu / DIGIWHIST / Government Transparency Institute (Mihály Fazekas); TED-based academic studies on software lock-in (e.g. Microsoft lock-in in procurement, "vendor lock-in" in public procurement studies, Free Software Foundation Europe "Public Money Public Code" evidence); Cigref/Asterès methods (only as method reference); EuroStack/Bertelsmann estimates; CISPE studies on Microsoft licensing; academic work from e.g. University of Amsterdam, TU Delft, Oxford Internet Institute, Hertie School.
- Studies using payment/budget data (e.g. UK spend-over-£25k, French data.gouv DECP, Spanish PLACSP, German, Dutch "inkoopdata") to measure cloud vendor spend.
- Which CPV codes / taxonomies were used to define ICT and cloud (e.g. 72000000, 48000000, 72317000, 72400000, 30200000)?
- Any work mapping products to vendors via descriptions (named-entity / brand dictionaries)?
- Known pitfalls: framework agreements, call-off contracts, multi-lot, licences vs services, overestimation from ceiling values vs actual payments.

Constraints:
- Europe (and UK) primarily; include notable non-EU method references only if directly transferable. 2015–2026.
- Distinguish verified-in-primary-source vs second-hand.

input.prompt:
Research the methodological families used to measure or assess digital sovereignty, and the classifications/standards that make such measurements comparable across countries.

Context: for the Italian civic Osservatorio Nazionale Sovranità Digitale (osservatorio.mxmap.it) and its sub-project measuring Italian PA ICT spending on cloud/datacenters by jurisdiction (IT / EU / extra-EU; attributing jurisdiction to the product, not the reseller). The Osservatorio already uses a 4-bucket jurisdiction classification (mxmap) and a 5-level sovereignty scale (1 US global cloud … 5 native European infrastructure). We need a taxonomy of methods and the standards to align with.

Objective: (a) a taxonomy of method families with strengths, weaknesses, typical data sources and examples: composite indices; infrastructure measurement (DNS/MX, hosting, ASN, TLS CAs, IP geolocation); market-share estimates; surveys; procurement/spend analysis; trade-in-services / balance-of-payments flows (Eurostat, OECD TiSMoS, ICT services imports); assessment/certification frameworks (EUCS draft and its sovereignty requirements, French SecNumCloud, German C5, Spanish ENS, Italian ACN qualification levels QC1–QC4, Gaia-X labels, EU Cloud Sovereignty Framework); (b) any published literature reviews or meta-analyses of digital sovereignty measurement methodologies (academic papers, e.g. in Internet Policy Review, Telecommunications Policy, Policy & Internet); (c) classifications usable for comparability: CPV codes for ICT/cloud, UNSPSC, COFOG, Eurostat/OECD ICT sector definitions, ownership/control determination (ultimate parent, GLEIF Level 2, EU FDI screening definitions, "control" in EUCS high+ / SecNumCloud immunity criteria), jurisdiction coding schemes, extraterritorial-law exposure (CLOUD Act, FISA 702).

Key questions:
- What families exist and which are best for a spend-based measurement?
- How do leading frameworks define "sovereign" / "immune to non-EU law" (control, ownership thresholds, personnel, location)?
- Which classifications would let our numbers be compared with Tussell, TED-based studies, EuroStack, Eurostat?

Constraints:
- 2018–2026. Exclude re-describing MxMap/CAmap, EDRIX, Nextcloud DSI, SEAL in detail (just reference them in the taxonomy).
- Distinguish verified-in-primary-source vs second-hand.

  This was a quick pass (about 12 calls) and I didn't read any primary source in full: all figures below come from press or summaries. The Bundestag PDF (Drucksache 21/5006) couldn't be extracted as text. Notes saved to `C:\Users\admin\osservatorio-nazionale-sovranita-digitale\progetti\spesa-ict\research_notes\Misure europee sovranità digitale\analisi_nazionali.md`.
  
  **Main finding:** no national body I found calculates the share of public ICT or cloud spend going to EU versus non-EU vendors. The only spend-by-vendor series are German parliamentary answers and the French Cour des comptes report of 22/10/2026. The audit offices (NL, CH, DK) measure contracts and risk, not spending.
  
  **Germany: government answers to the Bundestag** (Drucksache 21/5006 and 21/5413, 2026)
  - Federal spending on Microsoft: 74 M€ (2017), 198 M€ (2023), 204.5 M€ (2024), 481.4 M€ (2025, licences only).
  - An answer to a written question from the Greens gives different figures for the same years: 274.1 M€ (2023) and 347.7 M€ (2024). It covers more bodies (direct and indirect federal administration plus grant recipients). The government itself says comparability with earlier answers is limited.
  - Licences are counted through the central framework contract run by the Zentralstelle IT-Beschaffung, so effectively by product rather than by reseller.
  - Licence spending by ministry in 2025: Finance about 253 M€, Interior about 160 M€, Defence about 94 M€. Security agencies were withheld on "Staatswohl" grounds.
  - Oracle: total contract volume 4.8 bn€, including one contract of 4.6 bn€ (2023–2030). Two Microsoft framework contracts total 1.3 bn€ (Computerwoche, date uncertain, around 2023–24).
  - The only Bundesrechnungshof criticism of Microsoft dependence I found is from its 2007 annual report. I did not find the PwC 2019 study for the BMI.
  
  **Netherlands: Algemene Rekenkamer, "Het Rijk in de cloud" (January 2025)**
  - An inventory of cloud services, not of spending.
  - 84 of the 126 most important public cloud services (67%) have no risk assessment.
  - More than half of them are bought from Amazon, Microsoft and Google.
  - Three major contracts, including Microsoft 365 at the shared IT service centre (SSC-ICT), lack sovereignty, continuity and data-protection safeguards.
  
  **France**
  - Cour des comptes report on the state's office and collaboration tools (22/10/2026):
    - Covers about 860,000 workstations.
    - The state spent about 100 M€ on office tools in 2025, excluding operators, hospitals and local authorities.
    - A free suite would cost up to 130 M€ a year less than Microsoft 365.
    - It recommends migrating within 3–4 years to a suite hosted by the state or by a SecNumCloud-qualified provider.
  - Senate inquiry on public procurement (chaired by Simon Uzenat), report of 9/7/2025. Microsoft was heard on 10/6/2025 about Office 365 and Azure for the Health Data Hub.
  - A decree of March 2025 gives the national digital agency (DINUM) oversight of ministries' SaaS contracts.
  
  **Switzerland: Federal Audit Office (EFK/CDF)**
  - Report 23766 on the federal cloud strategy (2024): the cloud tiering model is unclear and there are no principles for SaaS.
  - Audit of the Microsoft 365 migration for about 40,000 workstations (2024): a "mixed" assessment.
  - Swiss Government Cloud: estimated cost about 319 MCHF, with the overall economic benefit not yet shown.
  - Report on Microsoft 365 backup (October 2026): only unclassified data may be processed in Microsoft 365, and backup needs improving.
  - Press reports put federal spending with Microsoft at about 140 MCHF.
  
  **Denmark: Rigsrevisionen**
  - Report on state IT operations outsourcing (2016), with follow-ups in 2022 and 2023.
  - In 2023, 24 of the 72 contracts reviewed carried a risk of vendor dependence.
  
  **United Kingdom: Computer Weekly analysis, not an official body**
  - 2023/24 spending: 55% of the £17.7bn spent with major tech suppliers (£9.9bn) went to hyperscalers or their resellers.
  - This grouping of resellers with the product is the approach closest to the Osservatorio's.
  - On the government's G-Cloud framework, AWS earned more than twice what Microsoft did.
  - I found no specific NAO or PAC report.
  
  **EU**
  - I found no European Court of Auditors report on cloud dependence.
  - Context only: a Commission tender worth 180 M€ for sovereign cloud services, assessed against its Cloud Sovereignty Framework.
  
  **Declared limits that recur:**
  - The set of bodies covered changes between answers or reports (Germany).
  - Large exclusions, such as operators, hospitals and local authorities (France).
  - Data withheld for security agencies (Germany).
  - Figures not comparable across years.
  
  **Not yet covered:**
  - Primary texts to read: Drucksache 21/5413, the Cour des comptes report, the Senate report, and the full Rekenkamer report.
  - Countries and bodies not searched or not found:
    - the PwC/BMI 2019 study
    - NAO/PAC (UK)
    - Riksrevisionen (SE)
    - Tribunal de Cuentas (ES)
    - Rechnungshof (AT)
    - SLM Rijk and Strategic Vendor Management (NL)
    - Schleswig-Holstein
    - the Danish digitalisation agency
  - I identified no named contacts, open data or code for any of these analyses.
</agent-message>

    - Its headline "over 80% of digital technology is imported" is taken from the Draghi report, and no calculation method is published. Avoid it as a benchmark.
    - Other figures: about 70% of foundation AI models come from the US; EU firms do about 7% of global software and internet R&D; the proposed plan costs about €300bn over 10 years.

  - **EU Institute for Security Studies (November 2025)** gives European providers 22% in 2017, which does not match Synergy's 29%.
  - **Digital Dependence Index (University of Bonn, with the Vodafone Institute):** 51 countries, 2017–2023, scored 0–1 where higher means more dependent.

A Vodafone advocacy piece (March 2026) says the surplus turns into a deficit if Ireland is excluded; this needs checking against Eurostat. Either way, balance-of-payments figures are a poor guide to which jurisdiction a product belongs to.
  - **Eurostat:** 52.74% of EU enterprises bought cloud services in 2025, ranging from 79.2% in Finland to 17.8% in Bulgaria. It is open data, but it covers enterprises only and measures adoption, not supplier jurisdiction.

  - **No relevant results found:** targeted searches for EPRS, European Court of Auditors, Interface and OpenForum Europe work turned up nothing relevant.
  - **Still open:**
    - whether DESI / Digital Decade has any supplier-jurisdiction indicator;

  - **Order-of-magnitude check:** balance-of-payments imports of ICT services (EBOPS 2010 categories).

  - **Correction:** TiSMoS is a WTO dataset, not OECD. OECD and Eurostat data are only inputs to it.

  - **C5, ENS, Gaia-X:** not researched; only my background knowledge is noted.

  - **Other schemes:** EBOPS SI for balance-of-payments data, COFOG for the public body's function, and the OECD ISIC definition of the ICT sector.   - **Literature reviews:** I found only the Fratini et al. review (271 articles) via search results; I did not retrieve the paper. Kaloudis 2022 and Shashkov et al. are known from abstracts only.   **Part A: studies**
  - **Compass Lexecon for the Open Cloud Coalition (24 July 2025), "Quantifying EU Public Sector Dependence on Productivity Software".** This is the only study I found that measures EU public-sector dependence from procurement data.
    - Data and coverage: TED tenders that mention Microsoft (189 of them, per Computer Weekly [S]), plus Statista. It covers the EU, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and Poland.
    - Results: Microsoft holds 73–80% of productivity software and up to 92% of office suites. Its share of TED tender mentions is 72–91% in 2023 and 89–100% in 2024.
    - Caveats: the press release gives no CPV codes, no keyword method and no individual authors. I did not open the full report. The coalition is backed by Google, and Microsoft calls it an astroturf campaign.
    - It counts mentions of a brand in tenders, not awarded amounts, so it is a coarser measure than our product-by-jurisdiction spend.
  - **European Parliament ITRE study PE 778.576 (December 2025).**
    - Authors: Vaida Gineikyte-Kanclere, Militsa Eggert and Goda Skiotyte, all of Visionary Analytics.
    - Advisory board: Paul Timmers and Roxana Radu. Responsible administrator: Anne Plöger.
    - Contact: ecti-poldep-b@europarl.europa.eu.
    - Method: desk research and interviews, with no analysis of public procurement data. Its figures are second-hand, for example about 80% of corporate software and cloud spend going to US vendors and a €264bn yearly "digital bill".
  - **CISPE / Frédéric Jenny (2023).** Estimates about €1bn a year in Microsoft licensing surcharges for SQL Server and about €560m a year for Office 365. It is based on licence prices, not procurement, and these are the claimant's own estimates.
  - **University of Bern study of Swiss IT procurement.** 2,754 IT projects on Swiss procurement data over seven years; 47.2% of those above the WTO threshold were awarded without a tender, and the paper proposes a way to measure vendor lock-in. I did not confirm the authors (I believe Matthias Stürmer et al.).
  - **Indices that are not based on spending, useful for comparison:**
    - EDRIX, by Stéfane Fermigier (Abilian, CNLL, APELL): five pillars, none on procurement.
    - Nextcloud Digital Sovereignty Index: counts self-hosted servers found via Shodan for about 50 tools; code is on GitHub.
    - Bonn Digital Dependence Index 2.0: 51 countries, run by CASSIS and the Vodafone Institute.
  - **CAmap is not Canadian.** The MxMap README lists it as "CAmap Nordic & Baltic", which maps how sovereign the TLS certificate authorities are. Its page returned 404 when I checked.

  **Germany, Drucksache 21/5006 and 21/5413 (Bundestag questions and answer)** [P, read the full answer]
  - The 481.4 M€ appears only in the preamble of Die Linke's question, quoting the Stuttgarter Zeitung. The question also quotes press figures of 74 M€ (2017), 198 M€ (2023) and 204.5 M€ (2024). The government's answer does not confirm any of these.
  - What the government actually gives (answer to Q1) is total 2025 software licence spend for all vendors, by ministry. The largest are the Foreign Office (AA) 253.2 M€, the Finance Ministry (BMF) 160.0 M€ and BMBFSFJ 94.3 M€. BMF's figure includes ITZBund, the federal IT service centre.
